issue: Period term softened: source "The savage tribes on our Western frontier" rendered "The Indian tribes". STYLE-NOTE (Period language) keeps period terms as printed.
replacement: Though a wide ocean separates the United States from Europe, there are various considerations that warn us against excessive confidence or security. On one side of us, stretching far to our rear, are growing settlements under the dominion of Britain. On the other side, extending to meet the British settlements, are colonies and establishments under the dominion of Spain. This situation, together with the nearness of the West India Islands belonging to these two powers, creates between them a common interest in regard to their American possessions and in relation to us. The savage tribes on our Western frontier ought to be regarded as our natural enemies and their natural allies, because they have most to fear from us and most to hope from them. Improvements in the art of navigation have, in making communication easier, made distant nations in great measure neighbors. Britain and Spain are among the principal maritime powers of Europe. A future agreement of aims between these nations ought not to be regarded as improbable. The growing distance of the blood relationship is every day weakening the force of the family compact between France and Spain, and politicians have always, with great reason, considered ties of blood to be feeble and uncertain links of political connection. Taken together, these circumstances warn us not to be too sanguine in thinking ourselves entirely out of the reach of danger.

issue: Source "The proprietary of this remark" (= propriety, aptness) rendered "The fairness of this remark"; sense is correctness/justice, not fairness.
replacement: It has indeed been put forward in the vaguest and most general form, supported only by bold assertions, with no appearance of argument and not even the backing of theoretical opinion. It contradicts the practice of other free nations and the general sense of America, as expressed in most of the existing constitutions. The correctness of this remark will be plain the moment we recall that the objection turns on a supposed need to restrain the LEGISLATIVE authority of the nation in the matter of military establishments. That principle is unheard of except in one or two of our State constitutions, and all the rest reject it.

issue: Three small drifts. Source "All violent policy, as it is contrary to the natural and experienced course of human affairs, defeats itself" (forced, unnatural policy) became "Any policy of violence", which changes the sense to policy using violence. Source "from the existence of partial disorders in one or two of her counties" lost "partial" (local, limited). Source "which will sometimes render a military force in time of peace essential" lost the qualifier "sometimes".
replacement: Any policy that does violence to the natural and well-known course of human affairs defeats itself. Pennsylvania offers an example of this right now. Her Bill of Rights declares that standing armies are dangerous to liberty and ought not to be kept up in time of peace. Yet in a time of profound peace, because of local disorders in one or two of her counties, Pennsylvania has resolved to raise a body of troops, and she will in all probability keep them up as long as the public peace appears to be in any danger. Massachusetts offers a lesson on the same subject, though on different ground. That State was compelled to raise troops to put down a domestic insurrection, and she did so without waiting for the approval of Congress that the Articles of Confederation require. She still keeps a corps in pay to prevent the spirit of revolt from reviving. The particular constitution of Massachusetts put no obstacle in the way of this measure. But the case still teaches us that situations are likely to arise under our government, as under those of other nations, in which a military force in time of peace will sometimes be essential to the security of society, and that it is therefore improper in this respect to control the legislature's discretion. Applied to the United States, it also shows how little the rights of a weak government are likely to be respected, even by its own constituents. And it shows us, besides, how poorly matched parchment provisions are against public necessity.

issue: Source "the greatest part of its most formidable pretensions"; candidate "most of its most formidable claims" is clumsy.
replacement: In England, for a long time after the Norman Conquest, the authority of the monarch was almost unlimited. Inroads were gradually made on the prerogative in favor of liberty, first by the barons and afterward by the people, until the greater part of its most formidable claims died out. But it was not until the revolution of 1688, which raised the Prince of Orange to the throne of Great Britain, that English liberty completely triumphed. As an incident of the undefined power of making war, which was an acknowledged prerogative of the crown, Charles II had, on his own authority, kept a body of 5,000 regular troops on foot in time of peace. James II increased this number to 30,000, who were paid out of his civil list. At the revolution, to abolish the exercise of so dangerous an authority, an article was included in the Bill of Rights then drawn up, that "the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, UNLESS WITH THE CONSENT OF PARLIAMENT, was against law."

issue: Pre-flagged "national" -1: source "the national exigencies" rendered "the nation's emergencies"; STYLE-NOTE keeps "national" as printed. Meaning unchanged, restore the word.
replacement: In that kingdom, when the pulse of liberty was at its highest pitch, no security against the danger of standing armies was thought necessary beyond a prohibition on raising or keeping them up by the mere authority of the chief executive. The patriots who brought about that memorable revolution were too temperate and too well informed to think of any restraint on the legislative discretion. They knew that a certain number of troops for guards and garrisons was indispensable; that no precise limits could be set to national emergencies; that a power equal to every possible contingency must exist somewhere in the government; and that, when they referred the exercise of that power to the judgment of the legislature, they had reached the furthest point of precaution that was consistent with the safety of the community.

issue: Silent repair of a probable source slip. Source: "it is an evil altogether unlikely to attend us in the latter situation" (literally the disunited state, evidently meant as the united one). Candidate silently changed to "the former situation". A source slip stays as read; listed as open issue.
replacement: But it is an evil far less likely to befall us in a united state than in a disunited one. Indeed, it may safely be asserted that it is an evil altogether unlikely to befall us in the latter situation. It is not easy to imagine that dangers so formidable could assail the whole Union as to require a force large enough to put our liberties in the least jeopardy, especially if we take into account the aid to be had from the militia, which ought always to be counted on as a valuable and powerful auxiliary. But in a state of disunion, as has been fully shown elsewhere, the opposite supposition would become not only probable but almost unavoidable.

issue: Source glitch "will, in its will, in its proper place, be fully detected" silently smoothed to a clean sentence; also "detected" became "exposed". Per brief, a source glitch stays as the source reads (open issue). Lead may decide to keep the smoothed form.
replacement: 1. The sophistry that has been used to show that this will tend to the destruction of the State governments will, in its will, in its proper place, be fully detected.

issue: "forced to resort to force" repeats the root awkwardly; source "necessitated to resort to force".
replacement: It cannot be denied that cases may arise in which the national government is compelled to resort to force. Our own experience has confirmed the lessons taught by the examples of other nations: emergencies of this sort will sometimes arise in all societies, however constituted. Seditions and insurrections are, unhappily, maladies as inseparable from the body politic as tumors and eruptions are from the natural body. The idea of governing at all times by the simple force of law, which we have been told is the only admissible principle of republican government, has no place except in the daydreams of those political doctors whose cleverness scorns the lessons of experience.

issue: Silent repair of a probable source misprint: source reads "the national presumption is that they would be ready to do their duty" (probably "natural"); candidate printed "the natural presumption". Pre-flagged national -1. Keep as source reads; open issue.
replacement: Should such emergencies ever arise under the national government, there could be no remedy but force. The means used must be proportioned to the extent of the harm. If it were a slight commotion in a small part of a State, the militia of the rest of the State would be adequate to put it down, and the national presumption is that they would be ready to do their duty. An insurrection, whatever its immediate cause, ultimately endangers all government. Concern for the public peace, if not for the rights of the Union, would lead the citizens to whom the contagion had not spread to oppose the insurgents. And if the general government were found in practice to promote the prosperity and happiness of the people, it would be irrational to believe they would be unwilling to support it.

issue: Addition: "we are told" is not in the source ("That of New Hampshire is to be marched to Georgia ...").
replacement: A sample of this appears in the exaggerated and improbable claims that have been made about the power of calling for the militia's services. The militia of New Hampshire is to be marched to Georgia, that of Georgia to New Hampshire, that of New York to Kentucky, and that of Kentucky to Lake Champlain. Indeed, the debts owed to the French and Dutch are to be paid in militiamen instead of louis d'ors and ducats. At one moment there is to be a large army to crush the liberties of the people. At another, the militia of Virginia are to be dragged five or six hundred miles from their homes to tame the republican stubbornness of Massachusetts, while Massachusetts's militia are to be carried the same distance to subdue the unruly haughtiness of the aristocratic Virginians. Do the people who rave in this fashion imagine that their art or eloquence can make the people of America accept any fancy or absurdity as infallible truth?
